title: Pre-Anesthesia Assessment
summary: Assess an elective patient in the pre-operative holding area and pass the key findings to the anesthesia team.
scenario: You are the anesthesia nurse in the pre-operative holding area. A patient is scheduled for elective surgery this morning. Complete a structured pre-anesthesia assessment and make sure the anesthesia team knows everything relevant before induction.
objectives: Identify the patient and procedure correctly
Follow a logical pre-anesthesia assessment workflow
Detect safety gaps in a pre-operative checklist
Communicate and document new allergy information
history: No chronic illness; no regular medication
Previous appendectomy under general anesthesia 10 years ago, no complications reported
Chart entry from booking: 'No known allergies'

steps.title: First contact
steps.prompt: The patient has just arrived in the holding area. What do you do FIRST?

options.text: Verify identity with two identifiers and confirm the planned procedure with the patient and the chart
Start examining the patient's airway
Ask the patient to sign the consent form straight away
Give premedication to reduce anxiety

steps.explanation: Correct identification and confirmation of the planned procedure prevents wrong-patient and wrong-procedure errors. It comes before any assessment, consent discussion or medication.
steps.takeaway: Identify the patient and the procedure first. Every other step depends on it.

steps.title: Assessment workflow
steps.prompt: Arrange the pre-anesthesia assessment in a logical order.

items.text: Review medical, surgical and previous anesthesia history
Confirm allergies, current medication and other safety questions
Perform a focused physical examination, including the airway
Confirm informed consent is documented and understood
Record the assessment and communicate findings to the anesthesia team

steps.explanation: History guides what to look for on examination, and both guide which investigations are relevant. Consent is confirmed once the plan is clear, and the findings are recorded and communicated last. Institutions may vary slightly; this station follows a history, examination, investigations, consent, communication flow.
steps.takeaway: History first, examination second, then investigations, consent and communication.

steps.title: Checklist review
steps.instruction: Select every entry that is incorrect or unsafe.
steps.prompt: Review the pre-operative checklist below. Which entries need to be corrected before the patient goes to the operating room?

items.label: Identity band matches chart: name and date of birth checked
Planned procedure on the consent form matches the operating list
Fasting: last solid meal 4 hours ago, marked 'adequate, proceed'
items.why: Common ASA fasting guidance is at least 6 hours after a light meal and longer after a fatty meal. 4 hours is not adequate; the anesthesiologist must be told.

items.label: Allergy section: left blank ('will ask later')
items.why: Allergy status must be actively confirmed and recorded before anesthesia, never left blank.

items.label: Baseline vital signs measured and recorded

steps.explanation: Two entries are unsafe: fasting time that does not meet common guidance was marked adequate, and the allergy section was left blank. Both can lead to serious harm if not corrected before induction.
steps.takeaway: Never accept a checklist item as done unless it is verified and consistent with the facts.

steps.title: New allergy information
steps.situation: While you review the history, the patient tells you she had itching and a skin rash after taking amoxicillin as a child. The chart still says 'No known allergies'.
revealHistory: Patient reports rash and itching after amoxicillin (childhood)
steps.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Clarify the details (drug, reaction, timing), document it as a reported allergy and inform the anesthesia team before the case
options.consequence: The allergy is documented and flagged. The anesthesia team can take it into account when planning drugs for the case.

options.text: Write it in the notes but tell nobody, because the chart is already signed
options.consequence: It is documented, but the team may not see it in time. Documentation without communication leaves a gap.

options.text: Ignore it: a rash in childhood is unlikely to matter
options.consequence: The reaction stays unrecorded and the team is unaware of it.

options.text: Wait to see whether the surgeon asks about allergies
options.consequence: Nobody may ask, and the information stays with you.

steps.explanation: Any reported drug reaction must be clarified, documented and communicated. Even a reaction that seems minor changes which drugs the team will choose.
steps.takeaway: Reported allergy means clarify, document and communicate. All three.

steps.title: Follow-up: antibiotic prophylaxis
steps.situation: The team is now preparing routine antibiotic prophylaxis. The chart still reads 'No known allergies'.
steps.prompt: You remember what the patient told you. What do you do now?

options.text: Speak up immediately: tell the anesthesiologist about the reported reaction so it can be verified before any antibiotic is given
Stay quiet, because it is not your responsibility
Wait until the surgeon has finished
Give the antibiotic slowly and watch the patient

steps.explanation: Every team member is responsible for speaking up when patient safety information conflicts with the chart. The right moment is before the drug is given.
steps.takeaway: If you know something that affects safety, speak up before the action, not after.

steps.title: Investigations
steps.prompt: This patient is generally healthy with no chronic disease. Which statement about pre-operative investigations is most appropriate?

options.text: Tests should be selected based on the patient's clinical condition and the planned surgery, not ordered routinely for everyone
Every patient needs a full panel of blood tests, chest X-ray and ECG
No investigation is ever needed before surgery
Only the surgeon decides which tests are relevant

steps.explanation: Current practice advisories support selective, indication-based testing guided by the history, examination and type of surgery. Routine testing in healthy patients adds cost and false alarms without clear benefit.
steps.takeaway: Order and review tests for a reason, not by habit.

steps.title: ASA class
steps.situation: Summary: 38 years old, BMI 24, non-smoker, no systemic disease, no regular medication, planned elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
steps.prompt: Which ASA Physical Status class fits this patient best?

options.text: ASA I: a normal healthy patient
ASA II: a patient with mild systemic disease
ASA III: a patient with severe systemic disease
ASA IV: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life

steps.explanation: A healthy, non-smoking patient without systemic disease is ASA I. The final class is assigned by the anesthesiologist; your role is to give accurate information for that decision.
steps.takeaway: ASA class reflects systemic health, not the planned operation.

steps.title: Documentation
steps.prompt: Which entry best reflects good documentation of this pre-anesthesia assessment?

options.text: A legible, timed and signed record covering history, allergies, fasting status, airway findings, ASA class and what was communicated to the team
A verbal report is enough; writing can wait until after the case
Only vital signs, because the rest is in the surgeon's notes
Copy another patient's entry and change the name

steps.explanation: The record is the shared source of truth for the whole team. It must be accurate, complete, legible, timed and signed for this patient. Copying another entry risks serious errors.
steps.takeaway: If it is not documented, the next person cannot rely on it.
